judge_assessment.explanation: Independently confirmed. Graph A's data array in verify.json id 1 pairs 26 cartons with 12 bottles, and the difference query on id 2 returns 18−4 = 14, so both the read and the corrected rise are right; the app group's mean is (88+79+95+84+74)/5 = 420/5 = 84 and the non-user mean is (72+66+81+70+76)/5 = 365/5 = 73; and Graph C's signed change from the 1-hour student to the 6-hour student is 6.5 − 9 = −2.5 hours, which is why the stem insists on a signed number. The judge's finding that 'observational association, lurking variables, self-selection and random assignment are correctly distinguished' matches what I read: problem 3 asks for a lurking variable behind both ice cream and sunscreen, problem 6 attacks the eleven-point advertisement on self-selection, and problem 8 requires the randomized design that would settle it. I checked both dominant systemic findings directly. Problems 3, 6 and 8 — every open item on the sheet — each carry a manual entry whose desc states the acceptance criteria, and the Quick Answers bank prints '3. —', '6. —' and '8. —' for exactly those three and real values elsewhere, so no verified answer is hidden behind the manual glyph. final_response.md names all three PDFs and, unusually, lists what each manual item must contain. I found no defect to file.

strengths_to_preserve: Problems 2 and 7 plant the SAME error twice on different displays — reading the horizontal axis when the question is about the vertical one, giving 28 instead of 14 and 5 instead of −2.5 — and both traps are machine-checked as distinguishable. Repeating one misconception across two contexts is what makes it stick, and the second instance requires a signed answer, which is strictly harder.

The three displays are chosen to fail in three different ways: Graph A is the confounded pair (a lurking variable), Table B is self-selected (who chose the groups), and Graph C invites a reversed arrow. That gives problem 8 a real synthesis target rather than a fourth repetition.

Problem 4 is a find-and-fix on a STATISTICAL error rather than an arithmetic one — Ravi pooled all ten students and got 78.5 when the question was about the app group — and the trap expression in verify.json is the full ten-value pooled mean, so the wrong method is proved to produce exactly the number the stem quotes.

The study guide's third section is a rewriting drill with an explicit word list (out: causes, makes, leads to, raises; in: is associated with, tends to go with) plus the instruction to scope the claim to the data collected. That converts a slogan into a procedure a student can execute.
case_summary: An eight-problem misconception-analysis packet that does exactly what the focus asks and stops. Five numeric answers, all recomputed correct; three genuinely open items (3, 6, 8) all declared manual with acceptance criteria and model answers; three declared traps machine-proved distinguishable and printed in the key's common-wrong-answers block. The standards tagging is unusually careful — 8.SP.A.1 for the plot reading, 6.SP.B.5 for the means, 7.SP.A for the study-design item — and the grade level appears only on the answer key. Four pages, all gates green, no relation or builtin defects in the bank, and final_response.md names all three artifacts. The 32/32 is right; I found nothing to improve.
